script.opening: "Hi, so I’ve just moved and registered with you, and I take diazepam for my anxiety — my old doctor always sorted me a few. I just need you to put a prescription through; I’ve nearly run out and I get really bad without them. I know what works for me, I’ve been on them years. Can you just do it so I don’t have to go through it all again with someone new?"

facts.text: If gently explored: on diazepam regularly for years (not short-term), dose has crept up (tolerance), gets withdrawal-type symptoms when low (shakes, worse anxiety, sweats), and has been BUYING extra online when prescriptions ran short — plus regular evening alcohol. This is benzodiazepine dependence, not simple anxiety relief.

Abrupt cessation of long-term benzodiazepines risks withdrawal seizures; combining benzodiazepines with alcohol (and any opioids) is dangerous (respiratory depression/overdose). So neither a flat refusal (precipitating withdrawal/driving her to the online supply) nor simply prescribing on demand is safe.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the defensiveness masks shame and fear: she half-knows she’s dependent and is frightened of being labelled an addict or cut off cold. Underneath, the diazepam is medicating an unaddressed driver — a recent diagnosis of her child’s serious illness has spiked her anxiety, and she’s using the drug (and alcohol) to cope. She wants relief and to not be judged or abandoned.

The skill is the "dependence fork": neither just prescribe nor just refuse — acknowledge the dependence non-judgementally, ensure safety (no abrupt stop, address alcohol), offer a structured plan (a safe prescribing/withdrawal plan, gradual taper, support) and treat the underlying anxiety properly (SSRI, CBT).

Officially: a diazepam prescription today, no fuss. What is needed: a safe, non-judgemental response that neither abandons her (precipitating withdrawal/online buying) nor simply continues an escalating dependence — a bridging-safety plan, an honest dependence conversation, alcohol safety, and proper treatment of the anxiety and its driver.

ice.ideas: Diazepam is what works for her anxiety; the new GP should just continue it as the old one did.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — shame and fear of being labelled an addict or cut off cold (she half-knows she’s dependent and buys extra online); the diazepam and alcohol are masking spiked anxiety since her child’s serious-illness diagnosis.
ice.expectations: A prescription today. What she actually needs: a safe, non-judgemental plan that avoids abrupt withdrawal, addresses the dependence and alcohol, and treats the underlying anxiety and its trigger.

cues: "My old doctor always gave me a few / I get really bad without them" — tolerance and withdrawal; dependence, not simple anxiety.
Defensive, pre-empting refusal, buying online — shame and fear of being cut off; approach without judgement.
A current unnamed stressor — the driver behind the escalation (her child’s illness) waiting to be surfaced.

checkpoints.text: Recognises BENZODIAZEPINE DEPENDENCE (long-term use, tolerance/dose escalation, withdrawal symptoms, supplementing from online sources) rather than treating it as a simple anxiety-relief request

Takes the SAFE middle path of the dependence fork: neither prescribes on demand nor refuses flatly — explains why abrupt cessation is dangerous (withdrawal seizures) and why escalating supply is harmful, and offers a structured, supported plan instead (NICE NG215: agree a gradual, individualised reduction with regular review; do not stop abruptly)

Addresses the COMBINED RISKS: the danger of benzodiazepine + alcohol (and opioids: MHRA Drug Safety Update, March 2020 — potentially fatal respiratory depression) — respiratory depression/overdose — and screens/advises on the alcohol (AUDIT-C; NICE CG115); arranges safe bridging rather than leaving her to the online supply

Plans a gradual withdrawal/taper and proper anxiety treatment: a structured diazepam-equivalent reducing regimen with support (NICE NG215: gradual, individualised, agreed with her, with regular review; step size and pace per BNF, slowed or held if withdrawal symptoms flare; specialist drug service if high-dose or multi-source use), and evidence-based treatment of the underlying anxiety (NICE CG113 stepped care: psychological treatment such as CBT or guided self-help via NHS Talking Therapies, and an SSRI with sertraline considered first) instead of ongoing benzodiazepines, which CG113 reserves for short-term crisis use

Surfaces the underlying DRIVER (the hidden agenda): explores the recent stressor (her child’s illness), the role the drug/alcohol is playing, and her mental state/risk — treating the cause, not just the prescription

Responds without judgement or labelling: de-escalates the defensiveness, names dependence as a common, treatable problem (not a moral failing), and reassures her she will not be abandoned or cut off cold
Shares the decision and builds an alliance: respects her experience while being honest about safety, so she stays engaged rather than going elsewhere/online

Safety-nets and arranges continuity: a clear interim plan (e.g. a short safe bridging supply with a follow-up rather than a refusal — after verifying the dose from the Summary Care Record or the previous practice, issued as small dated supplies, because diazepam is a Schedule 4 (Part 1) controlled drug), an appointment to make the taper/treatment plan, alcohol support, when to seek urgent help, and documentation — obtaining the old records

worked.txt: "Thanks for being upfront with me. I’m not going to do either of the two things you might be bracing for — I’m not going to just snap the tablets off you, and I’m also not going to simply keep them rolling without us talking, because I’d be doing you a disservice. There’s a safer middle path, and I want to find it with you."

"Can I be honest? From what you describe — needing more over time, feeling rough without them, topping up when scripts run short — your body has become dependent on diazepam. That is incredibly common and it is NOT a moral failing or you being an addict in the way people mean it. It’s a medical thing, and it’s treatable. You’re not in trouble."

"Two safety things I can’t ignore. Stopping these suddenly can cause fits, so we never just stop — we come down slowly and safely. And mixing them with the evening drink can affect your breathing, which is genuinely dangerous, so we’ll look at that together too. That’s why I won’t leave you to buy them online — that’s the riskiest option of all."

"Can I ask what’s been making the anxiety worse lately? … Your little one’s diagnosis. Donna, that is so much to carry — of course you’ve been reaching for whatever takes the edge off. That makes complete sense. But you deserve something that actually treats the anxiety, not just numbs it while the dose climbs."

"So here’s what I’d suggest. I’ll give you a safe amount to bridge you now so you’re not in withdrawal — no cold turkey. Then we make a proper plan: a slow, comfortable reduction with support, and treatment that genuinely helps anxiety — a different kind of medication that isn’t addictive, and some talking therapy. We’ll sort the drinking gently too. And I’ll get your old records so I’m not flying blind."

"You know your body and I’m going to work WITH you, not do things to you. If you feel really unwell — bad shakes, confusion, or any fits — that’s urgent, ring us or 999. Let’s book you in properly this week to set the plan up, and I’m your doctor for this now — you’re not starting from scratch with a stranger each time. Does that feel like something you can work with?"

f.learning: A "just continue my diazepam" request from a long-term user with tolerance, withdrawal symptoms and online top-ups is benzodiazepine DEPENDENCE, and the examinable skill is the dependence fork: neither prescribe on demand nor refuse flatly. A flat refusal precipitates dangerous withdrawal (seizures) and drives her to the riskier online/illicit supply; unquestioning continuation entrenches an escalating, harmful dependence — especially with concurrent alcohol (benzodiazepine + alcohol/opioids risks respiratory depression). The safe path acknowledges dependence without judgement or labelling, ensures safety (no abrupt stop; address alcohol; safe bridging), and offers a structured gradual taper (NICE NG215; step size per BNF) plus proper treatment of the underlying anxiety (NICE CG113: CBT or guided self-help and an SSRI, sertraline first) rather than ongoing benzodiazepines. Verify the dose (Summary Care Record or previous practice) before issuing small dated supplies; the MHRA (Drug Safety Update, March 2020) warns of potentially fatal respiratory depression with benzodiazepines and opioids. The hidden agenda is shame and fear of being cut off, with the drug (and alcohol) medicating an unaddressed driver — here her child’s serious-illness diagnosis. Surface and treat the cause, build an alliance so she stays engaged rather than going elsewhere, obtain the old records, and safety-net withdrawal red flags with continuity of care.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG215 (medicines associated with dependence or withdrawal symptoms, 2022) · NICE CG113 (generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder, 2011, updated 2020) · NICE CG115 (alcohol-use disorders, 2011) · MHRA Drug Safety Update March 2020 · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive
knowledge.summary: Years of diazepam, a rising dose, withdrawal symptoms and online top-ups is benzodiazepine dependence. Do not stop it suddenly and do not simply continue it. Verify, bridge safely, address alcohol, plan a gradual taper, and treat the anxiety and what is driving it.

points.t: Long-term use, tolerance with dose creep, withdrawal symptoms when supplies run low (shaking, sweating, rebound anxiety, insomnia) and buying extra online. This is physical dependence, and a new patient asking for a routine repeat may not say so unless asked kindly.

Stopping long-term benzodiazepines abruptly risks withdrawal seizures and delirium, and drives people to illicit supply of unknown content. Continuing on demand entrenches dependence. The safe path: verify the dose, bridge with a short supply, and agree a plan.

Check the Summary Care Record or contact the previous practice to confirm dose and duration before issuing. Diazepam is a Schedule 4 (Part 1) controlled drug; issue small, dated supplies with a named prescriber while the plan is set up.

NICE NG215: agree a gradual, individualised reduction with the patient, with regular review and support; do not stop abruptly. Step size and pace per BNF, slowed near the end or held if withdrawal symptoms flare. High-dose or multi-source use may need the specialist drug service.

Benzodiazepines with alcohol cause additive sedation and respiratory depression. MHRA Drug Safety Update (March 2020): benzodiazepines with opioids risk potentially fatal respiratory depression. Quantify alcohol with AUDIT-C (NICE CG115).

NICE CG113: benzodiazepines only short term during a crisis. Offer stepped care for GAD: psychological treatment (CBT, guided self-help via NHS Talking Therapies) and an SSRI, with sertraline considered first. Explore what has made things worse recently and assess mood and risk.

model.text: Hello Ms Preadon, it’s Dr Lee. Welcome to the practice. I understand you’re calling about your diazepam. Tell me about it.

I take it for my anxiety. My old doctor always sorted me a few. I’ve nearly run out and I get really bad without them. I’ve been on them years. Can you just put it through so I don’t have to go through it all again?

I can hear you’re worried about running out, and I’m not going to leave you without. I do need to understand your situation, because your records haven’t reached us yet. Then we’ll agree a plan. Is that OK?
model.why: Defuses fear of being cut off and sets the agenda

model.text: I suppose. As long as I’m not left with nothing.
How long have you been taking it, and how much do you take in a usual day now?
Years. Every day. It’s crept up; I take more now than when I started.
What happens when you run low?
I shake, I sweat, the anxiety goes through the roof. I can’t sleep.
When prescriptions have run short before, how have you managed? Lots of people in your position find other ways, and I’m asking so I can keep you safe, not to judge.
model.why: Normalises to allow honest disclosure about sourcing

model.text: (Pause.) I’ve bought some online. Just to get by.
Thank you for telling me. Tablets bought online can contain something different or much stronger, so that’s important. Do you drink alcohol, or take any painkillers or other medicines?
model.why: Checks alcohol and opioids for combined risk

model.text: A few drinks in the evenings. No painkillers.
You said the anxiety has been bad. Has something made it worse recently?
model.why: Opens the door to the hidden driver

model.text: (Quiet.) My child’s been diagnosed with something serious. I can’t switch off.

I’m so sorry. That’s an enormous thing to carry, on top of a move. Of course you’ve been reaching for whatever takes the edge off. How low has your mood got? Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself?
model.why: Acknowledges the stressor and screens mood and risk

model.text: No, never that. I’ve got to be there for them. I’m just scared you’ll think I’m an addict and stop them.

I don’t think that. What you describe, needing more over time and feeling ill when you run low, means your body has become dependent on diazepam. That’s very common after years on it, it’s a medical problem, and it’s treatable. You’re not in trouble.
Two safety points. Stopping suddenly can cause fits, so we never do that. And diazepam with alcohol can slow your breathing, so the evening drinking needs to come down while you’re on it.
model.why: Explains withdrawal seizure and alcohol risks plainly

model.text: So you’ll still give me some?

Yes. Today I’ll check your dose with your old surgery and the national record, and then issue a short supply, a week at a time, so you’re not in withdrawal and you don’t need to buy online. Could you promise me you won’t use the online ones?
model.why: Safe bridging after verification; stops illicit supply

model.text: Yes. If I’ve got my own, I won’t need them.

Then I’d like to see you this week to plan a slow reduction, at a pace you have a say in. And to treat the anxiety itself: talking therapy, and an antidepressant that helps anxiety and isn’t addictive. What do you think?
model.why: Shared decision on taper and CG113 treatment

model.text: Slowly is OK. I’ve always wondered if I could come off them.
I think you can. There’s also support for parents going through a child’s serious illness, and I’d like to talk about that when I see you.
model.why: Addresses the driver and plans holistic support

model.text: If you get severe shaking, confusion, see or hear things that aren’t there, or have a fit, call 999. If you run short or feel worse, ring me rather than buying tablets. And please don’t drive if you feel drowsy.
model.why: Withdrawal red flags and driving advice

model.text: Can you tell me in your own words what happens next?
You check my dose, I get a week’s worth, no online ones, cut down the drinking, and I see you this week to plan coming down slowly.
Exactly. I’ll be your doctor for this, so you won’t have to explain it all again. Anything else you want to ask?
model.why: Continuity addresses her fear of starting over

model.text: No. Thank you. I was dreading this call.

social.t: Caring for a seriously ill child is a major stressor. Ask what support she has; the child’s treating team and charities can often offer family and carer support.
A recent move means lost support networks and a new practice. Continuity with one clinician matters.

legal.t: Diazepam is a Schedule 4 (Part 1) controlled drug. Prescriptions are valid for 28 days. Buying prescription-only medicines online from unregulated sellers carries the risk of counterfeit or different drugs.

DVLA: non-prescribed benzodiazepine use, or doses above BNF guidance, counts as misuse or dependence for licensing; the licence is refused or revoked for at least 1 year. If she drives, advise her of her duty to notify. It is also an offence to drive while impaired by any drug.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe only when you have adequate knowledge of the patient’s health and medicines. Verify through the previous practice or Summary Care Record.
Record the verified dose, the online use, alcohol, the bridging quantity, the agreed taper plan and the review date.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral) for anxiety; local drug and alcohol service if dose is high or supply is from several sources.

redFlags: Previous withdrawal seizures or confusion when supplies ran out
Heavy alcohol use or opioid use alongside diazepam
Suicidal thoughts or overdose risk; high-dose or multi-source supply
psychosocial: Evening drinking; fear of being judged
ice: Idea: diazepam works and the old GP just kept it going

playbook.diagnosis: “Your body has become dependent on diazepam. That’s common after years of use, it’s a medical problem and it’s treatable. It means we mustn’t stop suddenly, and we also shouldn’t just carry on without a plan.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your body has adjusted to having diazepam every day, so it protests when the level drops. That’s the shaking and panic when you run low. Coming down slowly lets it adjust back, step by step.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried I’d label you and stop them. I won’t. What I want is a plan that keeps you safe and actually treats the anxiety.”
management.psychosocial: Support around her child’s illness, continuity with one clinician, alcohol reduction, and no more online supply.
sharedPlan: Verify dose; short weekly bridging supply; no abrupt stop
Gradual taper agreed with her (NICE NG215; step size per BNF)
CBT or guided self-help and an SSRI for anxiety (NICE CG113); reduce alcohol
safetyNet: 999 for fits, confusion, hallucinations or severe shaking
Ring the practice rather than buying online; appointment this week

pitfalls.intro: The benzodiazepine request is a fork: prescribe on demand or refuse flatly, and you fail either way. The marks go to the safe middle path, delivered without judgement.

items.fail: Issuing a month’s supply because “she’s been on it for years”.
items.why: “Unsafe prescribing.” The dose is unverified, she is drinking and buying online.
items.fix: Verify the dose, issue a short supply, and plan review this week.

items.why: Abrupt withdrawal after long-term use risks seizures and pushes her to illicit supply.
items.fix: Bridge safely and explain why sudden stopping is dangerous.

items.fail: Never asking how she has managed when scripts ran short.
items.why: The online supply and alcohol are the biggest safety issues. Missing them misses the risk.
items.fix: Ask kindly: “Lots of people find other ways. How have you managed?”

items.fail: Using the word “addict” or a lecture on the dangers of benzodiazepines.
items.why: “Judgemental approach.” She came in expecting exactly that, and will disengage.
items.fix: Name dependence as a medical problem that is common and treatable.

items.fail: Focusing only on the drug and never asking what has made things worse.
items.why: Her child’s illness is the hidden driver; missing it leaves the anxiety untreated.
items.fix: “Has something made the anxiety worse recently?”

items.fail: No plan beyond “we’ll review when your notes come”.
items.fix: Appointment this week, withdrawal red flags, ring rather than buy online, teach-back.

wordPics.pass: Recognises dependence; avoids abrupt stop; gives a short supply; warns about alcohol; plans a taper and anxiety treatment; books follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: verifies the dose before prescribing; draws out the online purchase without judgement; uncovers her child’s illness and addresses it; names dependence as a medical problem; involves her in the pace of the taper; offers continuity; checks understanding.

avoid.instead: “I won’t leave you without, and I won’t just keep it going without a plan either.”

avoid.instead: “Your body has become dependent on it. That’s common after years, and it’s treatable.”
avoid.why: “Addict” confirms her fear and shuts down honesty.

avoid.dont: “I’ll do a month’s supply and we’ll look at it when your notes arrive.”
avoid.instead: “I’ll check your dose today and give you a week at a time while we plan.”
avoid.why: Large unverified supplies of a controlled drug, with alcohol use, are unsafe.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Years of diazepam, a rising dose, withdrawal symptoms and online top-ups is benzodiazepine dependence. Do not stop it suddenly and do not simply continue it. Verify, bridge safely, address alcohol, plan a gradual taper, and treat the anxiety and what is driving it.

points.t: Long-term use, tolerance with dose creep, withdrawal symptoms when supplies run low (shaking, sweating, rebound anxiety, insomnia) and buying extra online. This is physical dependence, and a new patient asking for a routine repeat may not say so unless asked kindly.

Stopping long-term benzodiazepines abruptly risks withdrawal seizures and delirium, and drives people to illicit supply of unknown content. Continuing on demand entrenches dependence. The safe path: verify the dose, bridge with a short supply, and agree a plan.

Check the Summary Care Record or contact the previous practice to confirm dose and duration before issuing. Diazepam is a Schedule 4 (Part 1) controlled drug; issue small, dated supplies with a named prescriber while the plan is set up.

NICE NG215: agree a gradual, individualised reduction with the patient, with regular review and support; do not stop abruptly. Step size and pace per BNF, slowed near the end or held if withdrawal symptoms flare. High-dose or multi-source use may need the specialist drug service.

Benzodiazepines with alcohol cause additive sedation and respiratory depression. MHRA Drug Safety Update (March 2020): benzodiazepines with opioids risk potentially fatal respiratory depression. Quantify alcohol with AUDIT-C (NICE CG115).

NICE CG113: benzodiazepines only short term during a crisis. Offer stepped care for GAD: psychological treatment (CBT, guided self-help via NHS Talking Therapies) and an SSRI, with sertraline considered first. Explore what has made things worse recently and assess mood and risk.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Welcomed her as a new patient; let her state the request; reassured she would not be cut off before asking questions.
Recent move, her child’s serious illness, alcohol, her fear of being judged.
Picked up “I get really bad without them”, the pause about sourcing, and the recent worsening.
Idea (diazepam is what works); concern (being labelled an addict and cut off); expectation (a prescription today).
Verify dose via previous practice and Summary Care Record; AUDIT-C; GAD-7 and mood assessment at the follow-up.
Benzodiazepine dependence; untreated GAD; depression; harmful drinking.
Withdrawal symptoms, alcohol and opioid co-use, online supply, suicidal thoughts.
Names benzodiazepine dependence kindly and explains what it means.
Verified short bridging supply; no abrupt stop; planned gradual taper (NICE NG215); CBT and SSRI for anxiety (NICE CG113).
Alcohol reduction; support for her child’s illness; stopping online purchase.
Appointment this week, withdrawal red flags to 999, ring rather than buy online, driving advice.

social.t: Caring for a seriously ill child is a major stressor. Ask what support she has; the child’s treating team and charities can often offer family and carer support.
A recent move means lost support networks and a new practice. Continuity with one clinician matters.

legal.t: Diazepam is a Schedule 4 (Part 1) controlled drug. Prescriptions are valid for 28 days. Buying prescription-only medicines online from unregulated sellers carries the risk of counterfeit or different drugs.

DVLA: non-prescribed benzodiazepine use, or doses above BNF guidance, counts as misuse or dependence for licensing; the licence is refused or revoked for at least 1 year. If she drives, advise her of her duty to notify. It is also an offence to drive while impaired by any drug.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe only when you have adequate knowledge of the patient’s health and medicines. Verify through the previous practice or Summary Care Record.
Record the verified dose, the online use, alcohol, the bridging quantity, the agreed taper plan and the review date.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral) for anxiety; local drug and alcohol service if dose is high or supply is from several sources.

redFlags: Previous withdrawal seizures or confusion when supplies ran out
Heavy alcohol use or opioid use alongside diazepam
Suicidal thoughts or overdose risk; high-dose or multi-source supply
psychosocial: Evening drinking; fear of being judged
ice: Idea: diazepam works and the old GP just kept it going
Concern: being labelled an addict and cut off cold
Expectation: a prescription today without going over it all again

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Your body has become dependent on diazepam. That’s common after years of use, it’s a medical problem and it’s treatable. It means we mustn’t stop suddenly, and we also shouldn’t just carry on without a plan.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your body has adjusted to having diazepam every day, so it protests when the level drops. That’s the shaking and panic when you run low. Coming down slowly lets it adjust back, step by step.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried I’d label you and stop them. I won’t. What I want is a plan that keeps you safe and actually treats the anxiety.”
management.psychosocial: Support around her child’s illness, continuity with one clinician, alcohol reduction, and no more online supply.
sharedPlan: Verify dose; short weekly bridging supply; no abrupt stop
Gradual taper agreed with her (NICE NG215; step size per BNF)
CBT or guided self-help and an SSRI for anxiety (NICE CG113); reduce alcohol
safetyNet: 999 for fits, confusion, hallucinations or severe shaking
Ring the practice rather than buying online; appointment this week

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The benzodiazepine request is a fork: prescribe on demand or refuse flatly, and you fail either way. The marks go to the safe middle path, delivered without judgement.

items.fail: Issuing a month’s supply because “she’s been on it for years”.
items.why: “Unsafe prescribing.” The dose is unverified, she is drinking and buying online.
items.fix: Verify the dose, issue a short supply, and plan review this week.

items.why: Abrupt withdrawal after long-term use risks seizures and pushes her to illicit supply.
items.fix: Bridge safely and explain why sudden stopping is dangerous.

items.fail: Never asking how she has managed when scripts ran short.
items.why: The online supply and alcohol are the biggest safety issues. Missing them misses the risk.
items.fix: Ask kindly: “Lots of people find other ways. How have you managed?”

items.fail: Using the word “addict” or a lecture on the dangers of benzodiazepines.
items.why: “Judgemental approach.” She came in expecting exactly that, and will disengage.
items.fix: Name dependence as a medical problem that is common and treatable.

items.fail: Focusing only on the drug and never asking what has made things worse.
items.why: Her child’s illness is the hidden driver; missing it leaves the anxiety untreated.
items.fix: “Has something made the anxiety worse recently?”

items.fail: No plan beyond “we’ll review when your notes come”.
items.fix: Appointment this week, withdrawal red flags, ring rather than buy online, teach-back.
